skills.name: Undefined terms & definitions
skills.wrong_turn: A definition must work both ways. "A square has four right angles" is true, but rectangles have them too, so it isn't a definition of a square.
skills.rule: A precise definition names the category, states what sets the object apart, and is reversible.

skills.name: Conditional statements
skills.wrong_turn: A false hypothesis doesn't make a conditional false. "If n > 5, then n > 3" is true, even though n = 1 fails the hypothesis.
skills.rule: "If p, then q" (p→q): p is the hypothesis, q the conclusion.

skills.name: Related conditionals
skills.wrong_turn: A true statement's converse isn't automatically true. "If it's a square, it's a rectangle" is true; "If it's a rectangle, it's a square" is not.

skills.name: Biconditionals
skills.wrong_turn: "If" is not "if and only if". "If x = 3, then x² = 9" is true, but x² = 9 doesn't force x = 3.
skills.rule: "p if and only if q" (p↔q) means p→q and q→p.

skills.name: Truth tables
skills.wrong_turn: In logic, "or" includes both. p ∨ q is true when p and q are both true, unlike "soup or salad" on a menu.
skills.rule: A truth table lists every combination of truth values and the value of the compound statement in each.

skills.name: Inductive vs deductive
skills.wrong_turn: Examples can't prove "always". Seeing 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 doesn't mean the next number is 32.
skills.rule: Inductive reasoning finds a pattern and makes a conjecture; deductive reasoning proves from accepted facts.

skills.name: Counterexamples
skills.wrong_turn: An agreeing example proves nothing. A counterexample must make the hypothesis true and the conclusion false.
skills.rule: A counterexample satisfies the hypothesis but not the conclusion.

skills.name: Detachment & syllogism
skills.wrong_turn: Don't run a conditional backwards. "If it's a cat, it's a mammal" and "Rex is a mammal" don't prove Rex is a cat.
skills.rule: Detachment: from p→q and p, conclude q. Syllogism: from p→q and q→r, conclude p→r.

skills.name: Properties of equality
skills.wrong_turn: Don't mix up = and ≅. Lengths are equal, AB = CD; the segments themselves are congruent.
skills.rule: Reflexive: a=a. Symmetric: if a=b, then b=a. Transitive: if a=b and b=c, then a=c.

skills.name: Algebraic proofs
skills.wrong_turn: Every line needs a reason, the first one too: "Given". Jumping from 2x + 6 = 14 to x = 4 hides two properties.
skills.rule: An algebraic proof justifies each step of solving an equation with a property.

skills.name: Two-column proofs
skills.wrong_turn: A reason must be a definition, postulate, property or proved theorem, never "it looks that way in the diagram".
skills.rule: Statements on the left, reasons on the right, from the given to what you must prove.

skills.name: Paragraph & flow proofs
skills.wrong_turn: A paragraph proof still needs every reason. "Clearly the angles are equal" is not a reason; name the theorem.
skills.rule: A flow proof links statements with arrows; a paragraph proof tells the same steps in sentences.

skills.name: Indirect proof
skills.wrong_turn: Assume the exact opposite. The opposite of "x > 5" is "x ≤ 5", not "x < 5".
skills.rule: Assume the conclusion is false, reason to a contradiction, and conclude it is true.

skills.name: Proof by induction
skills.wrong_turn: The inductive step alone proves nothing. If n2+n were odd, (n+1)2+(n+1)=n2+n+2(n+1) would be odd too, yet n2+n is always even: there is no base case.
skills.rule: To prove P(n) for all n≥1: prove P(1), then prove that P(k) implies P(k+1).

skills.name: Sets & Venn diagrams
skills.wrong_turn: Don't just add the two circles: |A∪B|=|A|+|B|−|A∩B|. With 20 in French, 15 in Spanish and 5 in both, 30 take a language, not 35.

skills.name: Quantifiers

steps.b: true or false over a set

skills.wrong_turn: The negation of "all swans are white" is "some swan is not white", not "no swan is white". The negation of ∀x,x>0 is ∃x,x≤0, not ∀x,x≤0.
